name: Matumbi
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Matumbi (matu1259) is not in the catalog. The four title-hits are all about Kimatuumbi tone analysed through abstract accent/metrical structure (Odden 1982 WCCFL 1; Odden 1985 Benjamins pp. 345-420, doi:10.1075/ssls.6.18odd; Pulleyblank 1983 Foris/De Gruyter doi:10.1515/9783112420102-014) or a ~30-language East Bantu tone/accent typology (Philippson 1991 thesis, print/ANRT only; theses.fr abstract read). None could be opened: Benjamins, De Gruyter, OUP, ScienceDirect, HathiTrust and WorldCat all bot-blocked or paywalled; Unpaywall reports all closed; neither the 1983 Foris nor the 1985 Benjamins volume is on archive.org; WCCFL 1 is print-only. What was read (open): Odden's own manuscripts from his OSU homepage (Vowel Length, African Tone, Bantu Phonology) — Kimatuumbi has a mora-counting lexical tone system with contour tones only on long vowels; no stress statement. Secondary open text (Clements & Goldsmith 1984, archive.org scanned) and lending snippets (Odden 1988; Pulleyblank 1986) confirm that the 'accent' in these titles is a tonal/metrical accent governing H placement and vowel-length distribution (long vowels only in penult/antepenult, 'strong foot'), not word stress; Pulleyblank 1986 groups Kimatuumbi with 'stress or pitch-accent languages'. The authoritative descriptions remain Odden 1996 (OUP grammar) and Odden 2026 'Matumbi Phonology' (Elsevier IELL), both paywalled and not in the item list. Priority for acquisition: Odden 1985 high (76-page accentual analysis), Pulleyblank 1983 and Odden 1982 medium (superseded by Odden 1985/1996), Philippson 1991 medium (Matumbi coverage unverified). Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and Google Books APIs were rate-limited, so discovery relied on Crossref, Unpaywall, Glottolog, theses.fr, Sudoc, archive.org and Wayback.

earlier_scan.source_named: Odden, David 1996. The Phonology and Morphology of Kimatuumbi. OUP; also Odden 2026 'Matumbi Phonology', Elsevier, doi:10.1016/B978-0-323-95504-1.00544-5. Both paywalled.

new_statements.quote: All P-zone languages are tonal (though Ndengereko is losing distinctive prosody under Swahili influence). In terms of tonal inventory, all languages restrict contour tones to heavy syllables, long vowels, and VN sequences in Yao and Mwera. [...] Matuumbi allows LL (cháchaandlka 'taste sour'), LH (mboópo 'machete') and HL (ı́/ jmba 'swell'), but generally avoids HH. [...] There is attraction of final H to a long penult in Matuumbi (m#boópo ← m#boopó 'machete') [...] Matuumbi shortens vowels which are too far to the left in an utterance. At the word level, stem vowels are generally shortened before the antepenultimate mora
new_statements.citation: Odden, David. 2003. Rufiji-Ruvuma (N10, P10-20). In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds), The Bantu Languages, 529-545. London: Routledge.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.3 Tone, pp. 534-535 (txt l.16625-16642); vowel shortening sec. 2.1, p. 531 (txt l.16455-16460)
new_statements.translation_language: English (OCR renders the lax vowels ɪ/ʊ as j/l)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Matumbi is described as a tone language (H vs L, contours only on long vowels/heavy syllables, tense-determined verbal tone, final H attracted to a long penult); contrastive vowel length is confined to the last three moras of the word and to phrase heads. The source makes no statement about word stress or accent for Matumbi at all; no fixed stress position is described.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; for length, the first of two long stem vowels shortens, reduplicant penults keep length, phrase-head shortening before a modifier
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level and phrase-level tone and length; citation forms and phrasal forms both given. The absence of a stress statement in Odden's accessible descriptions (2003 sketch, 1980 tone paper, 2006 encyclopedia snippets, three later mss) is an absence, not a claim; the fuller descriptions (Odden 1996, 2026) were not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Odden's 'Kimatuumbi'/'Matuumbi' (Kipatimu area, Kilwa District, Guthrie P13) = Glottolog Matumbi matu1259 (ISO mgw). The quoted 2003 chapter uses Matuumbi as its representative of P10 and its general sentence covers 'all P-zone languages'; the Matuumbi-specific data come from Odden's own fieldwork (Odden 1996). Krumm 1912 spells the language Kimatumbi. No dialect is distinguished in any source seen.

sources.note: First-hand sketch with Matuumbi as the representative of P10 (author's own data; refers to Odden 1996). Sec. 2.3 Tone, p. 534: 'All P-zone languages are tonal'; Matuumbi allows LL, LH, HL contours on heavy syllables, avoids HH; final H attracted to a long penult (p. 535). Sec. 2.1, p. 531: stem vowels shortened before the antepenultimate mora; long stem vowels shortened in phrase heads. No statement of word stress or accent for Matuumbi anywhere in the chapter (txt l.16325-17178; the only 'unstressed' is about Makonde, p. 531).

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.

sources.note: Not read. Per Clements & Goldsmith (1984, intro, open scanned at, lines 921-925): 'This hypothesis is difficult to reconcile with the recent studies of Luganda by Hyman (1982) and of Kimatuumbi by Odden (1982), where in both cases, the operation of tone rules appears to be crucially dependent upon the presence or absence of accents.' So the paper argues that Kimatuumbi tone rules refer to an abstract accent distinct from tone; it is about tonal accent placement, not stress. WCCFL 1 proceedings are not online (no DOI, not on archive. Largely superseded by Odden 1985 and Odden 1996.
